Trajectory/end-to-end evaluation inspects the whole execution path — retrieval, tool selection, and step-by-step reasoning — not just the final output.

## Answer

The limitations of public LLM evaluation benchmarks directly support the need for trajectory-based evaluation frameworks in several ways:

**Benchmarks measure isolated model performance, not real-world agent behavior.** Public benchmarks like GSM8K, HellaSwag, and MT-Bench [2] "were designed to compare base models in isolation" and "score knowledge breadth, code generation, math reasoning, commonsense completion, and dialogue quality. None of them factor in your data, tools, latency constraints, or the failure modes your users will run into." This limitation establishes why trajectory evaluation is necessary—[2] notes that "a model can top every benchmark on this list and still fail the task your agent was built to do."

**Output-only evaluation misses critical multi-step failures.** The trajectory framework addresses this gap by recognizing that [3] "a single user request triggers dozens of internal steps, tool calls, and reasoning loops before producing a final answer." Evaluating only the final output [3] "tells you nothing about whether the agent retrieved the right documents, selected the appropriate tools, or reasoned correctly at each step."

**Application-specific evaluation is required.** Because public benchmarks fail to predict real-world performance, [2] concludes that "to know whether the system is ready to ship, you need application-specific evals, golden datasets, and online evaluation that reflect your real users, data, and workflows"—precisely what trajectory-based frameworks provide.

## Key sources
- [2] LLM Evaluation Benchmarks: What They Measure & Miss — https://www.langchain.com/resources/llm-evaluation-benchmarks
- [3] LLM Evaluation Framework: Trajectories vs. Outputs — https://www.langchain.com/resources/llm-evaluation-framework

It also motivates agentic-misalignment safeguards, since models show non-zero misaligned behavior under goal conflict and attackers already use agents to orchestrate autonomous attacks.
Net: rising autonomous offensive capability plus demonstrated misalignment risk make trustworthy frameworks and safeguards necessary, not optional.

key_points: Verifiers are part of a hierarchical loop stack in loop engineering that includes agent, verification, event-driven, and hill-climbing loops to progressively automate work and improve agent performance.
Verifiers serve an evaluation function within the broader loop engineering framework by assessing agent outputs, particularly for complex tasks like legal work.
Verifier efficiency is critical because verifier costs can be a bottleneck when running agent evaluations and reinforcement learning post-training at scale.
Verifier costs can be reduced by an order of magnitude through optimization techniques including batching, using open-source models, and prompt tuning while maintaining acceptable accuracy.
The verification loop operates within a hierarchical feedback system where human oversight can be strategically applied at different levels to build more reliable AI agents.
RubricMiddleware enables agents to self-evaluate against defined success criteria, while the human judgment approach incorporates domain expert input into the agent improvement loop.
RubricMiddleware focuses on iterative self-correction of agent outputs, whereas the human judgment guide emphasizes leveraging tacit domain expertise and institutional knowledge from team members.

RubricMiddleware addresses agents that produce outputs heading in the right direction but falling short, while the human judgment approach strategically incorporates human review into an iterative improvement loop.

RubricMiddleware is a feature within Deep Agents that automates evaluation and correction, whereas the human judgment approach combines automated evaluations with strategic human review of specific agent components.
Traces capture agent behavior and serve as the foundation for the agent improvement loop by enabling evaluation, annotation, and targeted improvements.
Traces are collected from production and other sources, then enriched with automated and human evaluations to identify failure patterns.
Better-Harness uses evals as a learning signal analogous to training data in machine learning, sourcing evals from production traces.
Evals encode the desired agent behavior in production and function as a gradient that guides iterative improvements to the agent system.
The improvement loop enables autonomous hill-climbing with human oversight, where each cycle generates better data and more reliable iteration before deployment.
A custom agent harness is the scaffolding that connects a model to real-world context, tools, and environments, with its effectiveness depending on how well it fits the specific task at hand.
Interpreter skills extend agent capabilities by combining TypeScript modules with skill instructions to enable deterministic workflows with greater reliability than model-driven execution alone.

Interpreter skills allow agents to spawn subagents and manage task graphs, enabling complex procedures to be executed in tested, reviewable code while maintaining model-driven decision-making flexibility.

Skills can direct the harness itself, not just the model, allowing the interpreter code to communicate directly with the agent loop while the model decides when to call skills and what inputs to provide.

Agent work becomes more easily evaluated when using interpreter skills because execution can be traced through deterministic code rather than relying solely on whether the agent generally followed instructions.

Tracing captures production observations of agent behavior, but traditional engineering metrics like latency and error rates are insufficient to detect quality issues like hallucinations and wrong answers.

Evaluation-based monitoring measures whether AI agent outputs are actually correct and useful by assessing output quality against domain expert standards, moving beyond infrastructure-focused metrics.
Domain expert review and annotation queues connect production traces to structured feedback, enabling subject matter experts to evaluate agent outputs and identify quality problems.
Problems discovered in live environments through evaluation become permanent tests that prevent the same failures from recurring, creating a feedback loop for systematic improvement.

The continuous improvement cycle integrates tracing (observation collection), evaluation (quality assessment), and domain expert feedback (annotation) to turn observations into actionable insights for engineers.
Project Fetch Phase Two demonstrates Claude Opus 4.7 can autonomously complete robotic tasks 20 times faster than the fastest human teams, showing significant autonomous task completion capability.

Project Fetch Phase Two identifies that Claude excels at programmatic tasks but struggles with precise physical control requiring closed-loop feedback, revealing specific limitations in autonomous physical agency.
The trustworthy agent framework requires managing risks from autonomous systems that can execute tasks across multiple applications with reduced human oversight.
The trustworthy agent framework addresses the risk that agents can misread users' intent and take actions with unintended consequences due to operating with less human oversight than chatbots.
The trustworthy agent framework must defend against prompt injection cyberattacks that attempt to trick models in autonomous systems.

The ATT&CK Navigator analysis identifies that highest-risk threat actors are distinguished by their ability to use AI agents for autonomous orchestration of multi-stage attacks, revealing the sophistication level that evaluation frameworks must test for.

SHADE-Arena is designed to test whether LLM agents can perform complex sabotage tasks while evading detection by monitoring systems, directly addressing the need to evaluate agent capabilities that the ATT&CK analysis shows threat actors are developing.

The ATT&CK Navigator introduces a novel risk-scoring framework for assessing AI-enabled cyber threats, which informs the design of evaluation frameworks like SHADE-Arena that must measure both sabotage capability and evasion of monitoring systems.

SHADE-Arena identifies important gaps in monitoring capabilities that need improvement as AI agents become more capable, reflecting insights from the ATT&CK analysis about the evolving sophistication of AI-enabled attacks.
AI agents in biology require redesigned infrastructure to function as reliable users, as demonstrated through the case study of viral sequence retrieval from NCBI Virus.
Current AI models struggle with inconsistent accuracy on biological data retrieval tasks, preventing them from reliably constructing datasets without additional support.
Adding deterministic retrieval layers (such as gget virus) dramatically improves agent performance on biological tasks, showing that infrastructure design directly enables agent reliability.
Building trustworthy agents across domains requires managing risks including agents misreading user intent and taking unintended actions due to increased autonomy.
AI agents are vulnerable to prompt injection cyberattacks that attempt to manipulate their behavior, representing a cross-domain security challenge for agentic systems.
Reliable agentic systems require a governance framework with technical defenses and industry-wide standards, not just individual domain solutions.

LLMs demonstrate step-change advances in exploit development capabilities, including converting vulnerabilities into exploit primitives and combining them into complete end-to-end attack chains, requiring evaluation metrics that capture multi-stage attack complexity.

LLMs can now discover high-severity zero-day vulnerabilities at scale in open-source code, indicating evaluation systems must distinguish between N-day and zero-day discovery capabilities rather than treating all vulnerability findings equivalently.

Generic benchmarks are insufficient for measuring production agent quality; evaluation metrics must be tailored to business-specific and security-specific requirements rather than relying on standard NLP metrics.

Production monitoring systems should connect evaluation traces to systematic improvements through human expertise, as one-off fixes are inadequate for managing evolving LLM cybersecurity capabilities.

Evaluation frameworks must assess whether agents meet domain-specific safety requirements like preventing misuse, not just measuring technical capability, given the dual-use nature of exploit and vulnerability discovery.
